solution:
The quantity of electricity that passes is \(Q = It\), which requires the time in SECONDS.

\(t = 2\,\text{h} = 2 \times 3600\,\text{s} = 7200\,\text{s}\)

\(Q = It = (0.5\,\text{A})(7200\,\text{s}) = 3600\,\text{C}\)

Conduction in a metallic wire is by electrons, and the charge on one electron is \(1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\). Hence the number of electrons is

\(n_e = \frac{3600\,\text{C}}{1.6021 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 2.25 \times 10^{22}\)

The same figure follows from the Faraday constant: \(3600/96487 = 0.0373\,\text{mol}\) of electrons, and \(0.0373 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 2.25 \times 10^{22}\).

Number of electrons flowing through the wire \(= 2.25 \times 10^{22}\).

A metal is extracted electrolytically when its cation has a very low (highly negative) standard reduction potential, so that no ordinary chemical reducing agent such as carbon, carbon monoxide or hydrogen is powerful enough to reduce it. The electric current then supplies the electrons instead.

For such metals the electrolyte must be the MOLTEN (fused) salt or oxide, not an aqueous solution: in water, \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) would be reduced at the cathode in preference to the metal ion, and hydrogen would be liberated instead of the metal.

Metals obtained in this way, with the melt used:

(i) Sodium, \(\text{Na}\) - electrolysis of fused \(\text{NaCl}\)

(ii) Potassium, \(\text{K}\) - electrolysis of fused \(\text{KCl}\)

(iii) Lithium, \(\text{Li}\) - electrolysis of fused \(\text{LiCl}\)

(iv) Magnesium, \(\text{Mg}\) - electrolysis of fused \(\text{MgCl}_2\)

(v) Calcium, \(\text{Ca}\) - electrolysis of fused \(\text{CaCl}_2\)

(vi) Aluminium, \(\text{Al}\) - electrolysis of \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) dissolved in molten cryolite

The cathode reaction in each case is simply \(\text{M}^{n+} + n e^{-} \rightarrow \text{M}\), for example \(\text{Na}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Na}\) and \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}\).

Electrolysis is also used to REFINE metals that have already been extracted chemically - copper, zinc, silver, nickel, tin and chromium - where the impure metal is the anode and the pure metal deposits on the cathode.

Metals extracted electrolytically: \(\text{Na}\), \(\text{K}\), \(\text{Li}\), \(\text{Mg}\), \(\text{Ca}\) and \(\text{Al}\) (from their fused salts or oxide); \(\text{Cu}\), \(\text{Zn}\), \(\text{Ag}\) and \(\text{Ni}\) are purified electrolytically.

The charge needed follows from the stoichiometry of the electrode reaction: \(Q = nF\), where \(n\) is the number of moles of electrons per mole of the species reduced.

The given half-reaction is

\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^{+} + 6e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

so \(n = 6\) mol of electrons per mole of \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\). (This is consistent with the oxidation states: chromium goes from \(+6\) to \(+3\), a gain of 3 electrons per \(\text{Cr}\) atom, and there are 2 chromium atoms in the ion.)

Taking \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\),

\(Q = 6 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 578922\,\text{C}\)

Quantity of electricity needed \(= 6F = 5.79 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\).

The lead storage battery is a secondary cell, so it is recharged by driving current through it from an external source in the direction OPPOSITE to that of discharge. Every step of the discharge reaction is then reversed and the cell is restored to its original state.

Materials involved: a lead grid packed with spongy lead (the negative plate), a lead grid packed with lead dioxide \(\text{PbO}_2\) (the positive plate), the lead sulphate \(\text{PbSO}_4\) that has been deposited on BOTH plates during discharge, water, and the electrolyte, about 38 per cent aqueous sulphuric acid \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\).

During discharge the reactions are

At the lead plate: \(\text{Pb(s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2e^{-}\)

At the \(\text{PbO}_2\) plate: \(\text{PbO}_2\text{(s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)

On RECHARGING the external source forces electrons into the lead plate and pulls them out of the \(\text{PbO}_2\) plate, so the roles of the electrodes are interchanged: the lead plate, which was the anode on discharge, is now the site of reduction, and the \(\text{PbO}_2\) plate is now the site of oxidation. The reactions are

Reduction, at the spongy-lead plate: \(\text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Pb(s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)}\)

Oxidation, at the lead dioxide plate: \(\text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{PbO}_2\text{(s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}\text{(aq)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-}\)

Overall reaction on recharging:

\(2\text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Pb(s)} + \text{PbO}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}\)

The insoluble \(\text{PbSO}_4\) on the two plates is therefore converted back into spongy \(\text{Pb}\) and \(\text{PbO}_2\) respectively, water is consumed and sulphuric acid is regenerated. Because the acid is put back into solution, the density (specific gravity) of the electrolyte rises as charging proceeds, which is how the state of charge of the battery is tested in practice.

Recharging reverses the discharge reaction: \(2\text{PbSO}_4\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Pb(s)} + \text{PbO}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}\), with \(\text{PbSO}_4\) reduced to \(\text{Pb}\) at the negative plate and oxidised to \(\text{PbO}_2\) at the positive plate, and \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) restored to the electrolyte.

A fuel cell is a galvanic cell in which the reactants are fed continuously to the electrodes, so any substance whose combustion is strongly exothermic and which can be oxidised at an electrode can serve as the fuel. Besides hydrogen, methane and methanol are the two most widely used.

(i) Methane, \(\text{CH}_4\). The overall cell reaction is its combustion,

\(\text{CH}_4\text{(g)} + 2\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)

(ii) Methanol, \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\). In an alkaline cell the electrode reactions are

Anode: \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH(l)} + 6\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + 5\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + 6e^{-}\)

Cathode: \(\tfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + 6e^{-} \rightarrow 6\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}\)

Overall: \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH(l)} + \tfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\)

Other fuels that have been used are carbon monoxide, \(\text{CO}\), and hydrocarbons such as propane and butane, all burnt at the anode against oxygen at the cathode.

Two materials other than hydrogen: methane \(\text{CH}_4\) and methanol \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\).

Rusting needs both water and air, and it is best pictured as an enormous number of tiny galvanic cells set up on the surface of the iron object. All four parts of a galvanic cell are present: an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte and an external circuit.

Anode: a strained, impure or exposed spot on the iron surface, where the metal is oxidised

\(2\text{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 4e^{-}\), \(\quad E^{\circ}_{(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe})} = -0.44\,\text{V}\)

External circuit: the iron object itself, which is a metallic conductor, carries the released electrons from this spot to another spot on the surface.

Cathode: that other spot, covered by the film of moisture, where dissolved atmospheric oxygen is reduced in the presence of \(\text{H}^{+}\)

\(\text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4e^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\), \(\quad E^{\circ} = 1.23\,\text{V}\)

The \(\text{H}^{+}\) needed here comes from carbonic acid \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\), formed when atmospheric carbon dioxide dissolves in the water film, and from other acidic oxides dissolved from the atmosphere.

Electrolyte and salt bridge: the thin film of water on the surface, made conducting by these dissolved gases and by any dissolved salts, which completes the circuit by carrying ions between the anodic and cathodic spots.

Overall cell reaction:

\(2\text{Fe(s)} + \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}\), \(\quad E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 1.23 - (-0.44) = 1.67\,\text{V}\)

The large positive \(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\) shows the process is spontaneous, which is why iron rusts of its own accord.

Finally the \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) ions that have gone into the water film are further oxidised by atmospheric oxygen to the ferric state, and the product separates as rust, hydrated ferric oxide:

\(2\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\text{(s)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)}\)

the oxide taking up water to give \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}\). The \(\text{H}^{+}\) regenerated in this step feeds the cathodic reaction again, so the corrosion is self-sustaining.

Rusting is thus an electrochemical cell in which iron is the anode, a moisture-covered spot reducing dissolved oxygen is the cathode, the water film containing dissolved \(\text{CO}_2\) is the electrolyte, and the metal itself is the external circuit; the \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) so formed is air-oxidised to hydrated ferric oxide, \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}\), which is rust.

For each reduction, write the balanced half-reaction, read off \(n\), the number of moles of electrons per mole of the ion, and use \(Q = nF\) with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\).

(i) \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}\), so \(n = 3\).

\(Q = 3 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 289461\,\text{C}\)

(ii) \(\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}\), so \(n = 2\).

\(Q = 2 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 192974\,\text{C}\)

(iii) In \(\text{MnO}_4^{-}\) manganese is in the \(+7\) state and in \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) it is in the \(+2\) state, a gain of 5 electrons per manganese atom, so \(n = 5\):

\(\text{MnO}_4^{-} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 5e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

\(Q = 5 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 482435\,\text{C}\)

Charge required:

(i) \(3F = 2.89 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\)

(ii) \(2F = 1.93 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\)

(iii) \(5F = 4.82 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\)

Electricity in faraday is the number of moles of electrons required, which is (moles of metal produced) \(\times\) \(n\), where \(n\) comes from the cathode half-reaction. Atomic masses used: \(\text{Ca} = 40\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Al} = 27\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

(i) Molten \(\text{CaCl}_2\) gives calcium by \(\text{Ca}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ca}\), so \(n = 2\).

Moles of \(\text{Ca} = \frac{20.0\,\text{g}}{40\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.50\,\text{mol}\)

Electricity \(= 0.50 \times 2 = 1.0\,F\)

(ii) Molten \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) gives aluminium by \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Al}\), so \(n = 3\).

Moles of \(\text{Al} = \frac{40.0\,\text{g}}{27\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 1.481\,\text{mol}\)

Electricity \(= 1.481 \times 3 = 4.44\,F\)

Electricity required:

(i) \(1.0\,F\) (about \(9.65 \times 10^{4}\,\text{C}\))

(ii) \(4.44\,F\) (about \(4.29 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\))

In each case find \(n\), the moles of electrons LOST per mole of the substance oxidised, from the change in oxidation number, then use \(Q = nF\) with \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\).

(i) Oxygen goes from \(-2\) in \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to \(0\) in \(\text{O}_2\), a loss of 2 electrons per oxygen atom. One mole of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) contains one mole of oxygen atoms, so \(n = 2\). The balanced half-reaction confirms it:

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4e^{-}\)

i.e. 4 mol of electrons for 2 mol of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so 2 mol of electrons for 1 mol.

\(Q = 2 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 192974\,\text{C}\)

(ii) Iron goes from \(+2\) in \(\text{FeO}\) to \(+3\) in \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\), a loss of only 1 electron per iron atom. One mole of \(\text{FeO}\) contains one mole of iron, so \(n = 1\):

\(2\text{FeO(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\text{(s)} + 2\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-}\)

i.e. 2 mol of electrons for 2 mol of \(\text{FeO}\), so 1 mol of electrons for 1 mol.

\(Q = 1 \times 96487\,\text{C} = 96487\,\text{C}\)

Electricity required:

(i) \(2F = 1.93 \times 10^{5}\,\text{C}\)

(ii) \(1F = 9.65 \times 10^{4}\,\text{C}\)

The platinum electrodes are inert, so at the cathode the nickel ion is discharged:

\(\text{Ni}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ni(s)}\), so \(n = 2\)

Charge passed, with the time converted to seconds:

\(t = 20\,\text{min} = 20 \times 60 = 1200\,\text{s}\)

\(Q = It = (5\,\text{A})(1200\,\text{s}) = 6000\,\text{C}\)

By Faraday's first law the mass deposited is \(m = \frac{ItM}{nF}\), with \(M(\text{Ni}) = 58.7\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\) and \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\):

\(m = \frac{6000\,\text{C} \times 58.7\,\text{g mol}^{-1}}{2 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}} = 1.825\,\text{g}\)

(Equivalently: moles of electrons \(= 6000/96487 = 0.0622\,\text{mol}\), moles of \(\text{Ni} = 0.0311\,\text{mol}\), mass \(= 0.0311 \times 58.7 = 1.825\,\text{g}\).)

Mass of nickel deposited at the cathode \(= 1.83\,\text{g}\).

The three cells are in SERIES, so exactly the same quantity of electricity passes through each of them. Find \(Q\) from the silver deposited in cell B, then use it for the time and for the other two metals. Atomic masses used: \(\text{Ag} = 108\), \(\text{Cu} = 63.5\), \(\text{Zn} = 65.4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\).

Cell B: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}\), so \(n = 1\).

Moles of \(\text{Ag} = \frac{1.45\,\text{g}}{108\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.01343\,\text{mol}\), which needs \(0.01343\,\text{mol}\) of electrons.

\(Q = 0.01343 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1} = 1295\,\text{C}\)

Time, from \(Q = It\):

\(t = \frac{1295\,\text{C}}{1.5\,\text{A}} = 864\,\text{s}\), that is \(14.4\,\text{min}\)

Cell C: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu(s)}\), so \(n = 2\) and the moles of copper are half the moles of electrons.

Moles of \(\text{Cu} = \frac{0.01343}{2} = 0.006713\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{Cu} = 0.006713 \times 63.5 = 0.426\,\text{g}\)

Cell A: \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn(s)}\), so \(n = 2\) likewise.

Moles of \(\text{Zn} = 0.006713\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{Zn} = 0.006713 \times 65.4 = 0.439\,\text{g}\)

Time for which the current flowed \(= 864\,\text{s}\) (\(14.4\,\text{min}\)); mass of copper deposited \(= 0.426\,\text{g}\); mass of zinc deposited \(= 0.439\,\text{g}\).
_note: Masses of Cu and Zn depend on the atomic-mass table used; with Cu = 63.5 and Zn = 65.4 the answers are 0.426 g and 0.439 g. NCERT's own worked Example 2.10 uses Cu = 63, which would give 0.423 g.

solution:
At each electrode the species with the more favourable potential is discharged: at the cathode the reduction with the HIGHER \(E^{\circ}\) is preferred, and at the anode the oxidation with the LOWER \(E^{\circ}\) is preferred, except where a large overpotential makes the thermodynamically easier process too slow to compete. Whether the electrode itself takes part also matters: platinum is inert, silver is reactive.

(i) Aqueous \(\text{AgNO}_3\) with silver electrodes.

Cathode: the competing reductions are \(\text{Ag}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}\) (\(E^{\circ} = +0.80\,\text{V}\)) and the reduction of water; silver, with much the higher \(E^{\circ}\), is discharged and silver metal is deposited.

Anode: the electrode is REACTIVE, and oxidising silver metal (\(\text{Ag} \rightarrow \text{Ag}^{+} + e^{-}\)) is easier than oxidising water to \(\text{O}_2\) (\(E^{\circ} = 1.23\,\text{V}\)). So the silver anode itself dissolves.

Silver is therefore simply transferred from the anode to the cathode and the concentration of the \(\text{AgNO}_3\) solution stays unchanged. This is the basis of silver plating and of electro-refining.

(ii) Aqueous \(\text{AgNO}_3\) with platinum electrodes.

Cathode: as before, \(\text{Ag}^{+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag}\); silver is deposited.

Anode: platinum is inert and cannot dissolve, and nitrogen in \(\text{NO}_3^{-}\) is already in its highest oxidation state \(+5\), so it cannot be oxidised. Water is oxidised instead:

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{O}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + 4e^{-}\)

Oxygen gas is evolved and the solution turns acidic.

(iii) Dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) with platinum electrodes.

Cathode: \(\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{(g)}\) (\(E^{\circ} = 0.00\,\text{V}\)); hydrogen gas is liberated.

Anode: the possibilities are \(2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4e^{-}\) (\(E^{\circ} = 1.23\,\text{V}\)) and \(2\text{SO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} + 2e^{-}\) (\(E^{\circ} = 1.96\,\text{V}\)). The lower value is preferred, so with DILUTE acid water is oxidised and oxygen is evolved. The net result is the electrolysis of water. (Only with concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) does peroxodisulphate form instead.)

(iv) Aqueous \(\text{CuCl}_2\) with platinum electrodes.

Cathode: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu(s)}\) (\(E^{\circ} = +0.34\,\text{V}\)) is preferred to the reduction of water, so copper is deposited.

Anode: the competing oxidations are \(\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2 + e^{-}\) (\(E^{\circ} = 1.36\,\text{V}\)) and \(2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^{+} + 4e^{-}\) (\(E^{\circ} = 1.23\,\text{V}\)). On potentials alone water should be oxidised, but the evolution of oxygen has a large OVERPOTENTIAL, so in practice chloride is discharged and chlorine gas is evolved.

Products:

(i) Cathode: silver deposited. Anode: the silver electrode dissolves as \(\text{Ag}^{+}\); no gas, and the solution concentration is unchanged.

(ii) Cathode: silver deposited. Anode: oxygen gas, and the solution becomes acidic.

(iii) Cathode: hydrogen gas. Anode: oxygen gas.

(iv) Cathode: copper deposited. Anode: chlorine gas.
